name: Mandelic acid

card.summary: A larger, slower-penetrating alpha-hydroxy acid used in gentle peels and serums for acne and dark spots; direct clinical evidence is thin.
card.aka: Alpha-hydroxy phenylacetic acid, AHA, mandelic peel
card.note: Studied mostly as part of formulations or in broader AHA reviews; few dedicated trials of mandelic acid alone.

quick.overview:
Mandelic acid is an alpha-hydroxy acid (AHA) used in skincare as a chemical exfoliant, mainly for acne, uneven pigmentation and sensitive skin. It is sold in serums and professional-strength peels.

A large Cochrane review covered AHA treatments for acne as a class. Dedicated mandelic acid trials are limited in the available literature; registered trials compare mandelic peels with tranexamic acid for melasma and test a combined peel for periocular rejuvenation.
quick.mechanism: Mandelic acid is described as having a larger molecular size than glycolic acid, which is said to slow skin penetration and reduce irritation. As an AHA it promotes exfoliation and cell turnover, and encyclopedic summaries describe antibacterial activity.
quick.risks: Common AHA effects are stinging, redness and peeling. The published literature give little mandelic acid-specific safety data. It has been studied as a natural preservative in emulsions, and sun protection is generally advised with AHA products.

lead: Mandelic acid (2-hydroxy-2-phenylacetic acid) is a chiral alpha-hydroxy acid with the formula C8H8O3 [1]. In cosmetics and dermatology it is used as a chemical exfoliant for acne, hyperpigmentation and photoaging [1].

An encyclopedic summary says it penetrates skin more slowly than smaller AHAs such as glycolic acid because of its larger molecule, and therefore causes less irritation, and cites formulation studies reporting acne lesion reductions of up to 69% [1]. That summary is AI-generated and its citations were not verified here.

Controlled clinical evidence specific to mandelic acid is sparse. A Cochrane review assessed topical alpha-hydroxy acids for acne as a group, and registered trials are examining mandelic peels in melasma and in a periocular peel [3][6][7].

paras: Cosmetic uses include chemical peels and serums for acne-prone, pigmented or photoaged skin, with exfoliation attributed to the acid's cell-turnover effect [1]. Mandelic acid is also studied as a natural preservative: a 2024 paper examined emulsions formulated with mandelic acid and essential oils as sustainable preservatives [5].

A 2020 Cochrane review of topical azelaic acid, salicylic acid, nicotinamide, sulphur, zinc and alpha-hydroxy acids for acne included 49 randomized trials with 3,880 participants and examined patient self-assessment, withdrawals, minor adverse events and quality of life; mandelic acid was not the review's sole subject [3]. A 2022 network meta-analysis of acne treatments covers other topical and oral options [2].

A registered trial of 120 participants (not yet recruiting) plans to compare intralesional tranexamic acid with a mandelic acid peel for melasma [6]. A completed phase IV registration of 12 participants evaluated a 'duosomal' chemical peel for aesthetic enhancement of periocular and facial regions [7]. A randomized trial of a peel formulated with polyhydroxy acids across skin types, including sensitive skin, is a different acid class [4]. No large randomized trial of mandelic acid alone for acne or pigmentation is available in the published literature.
Encyclopedic summaries describe mandelic acid as gentler than smaller AHAs [1]. The published literature contain no mandelic acid-specific safety trial.

A 2005 T Nation thread on fighting acne includes one user's report that a mandelic acid lotion helped their acne [8]. This is an individual anecdote; looksmaxxing forums are not otherwise documented to discuss it in the available sources.
